title: The Dixieland bass: keeping the beat and the root of the chord
summary: Breaux explains that the Dixieland bass stays on the root of the chord, unlike a big band bass, and why correct chords matter.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: I mean I'll play it because it paid me but I prefer Dixon Land for actual personal enjoyment you might say. Well I mean I like ballads thrown along in there but I mean actually for what you call stomped down jumping, a good Dixon Land band you just can't get around because you always have that absolute beat and that's very essential with that type of music.

In regard to your bass, do you notice that the New Orleans players on bass play different than other styles of music? Is there any certain style that you'd say makes the Dixieland rather than ordinary big band bass? I'd say that Ellington, of course your cousin played in Ellington too, but I mean ordinarily is there any difference?

Well I mean the average Dixieland bass player as I notice as I gather, he's always playing the root of the chord, I mean it's just, you have to, to make it fit in right. Now if you take a big band, after a band gets to be around 12 pieces or more, well whoever's arranging can take the bass off the basic note of the chord and place it somewhere else according to how he's voicing, how he's voicing his instrumentation. And sometimes you hear a bass playing completely almost off the chord if you, unless you just actually know the arrangement and know how it's built. But Dixieland, the bass, we always call it, I mean I do call it the bottom, he always stays in the cellar, he's always bringing the basic note of the particular chord that's supposed to be played.

When you think of your job in a band, in a small Dixieland band, do you think of it more like that? To keep the beat going or is it to fill in the harmony of the chords or what do you think of yourself?

Well I mean I like to keep the beat going but I like to keep the right chords going too because I mean it's very effective. I mean a lot of people don't realize it, probably I mean people unless they're musicians wouldn't know the difference. But I mean it's a big difference if you're playing just as simple, I would say something in C. And you got a bass man up there that probably is not paying attention to what he's doing or maybe they'll know what he's doing, I'll put it that way too. And you playing something in C, he's reaching down there and playing a D flat, a big D flat against a C major chord, well I mean that don't work out at all, no kind of way. And it's very important for the bass to, especially in Dixieland, to keep the basic note of the chord going at all times regardless. Because if the public could know what the musician he's playing was he'll let them know maybe after they get through the number they'll let them know in not such a sweet tongue.
